passage: Note, Friday, by Jagdish, counsellor. Yogesh came in on Monday looking determined: he had deleted every game and social app the night before and swore he would never open them again. I said it was a brave start, but I asked what he would do on a bad day. He said he would not have any. On Friday he came in silent. On the fourth night he had reinstalled one app to check a group message and then, "since I already failed", stayed on it until two. He said he felt there was no point trying now. I told him one slip is information, not a verdict, and asked him to bring a smaller plan next week.

passage:
Saturday, 1 am
Day five. Or day zero again. On Monday I deleted every game and every social app, told Kalyani Didi I was "free now", and wrote NO SCREENS in marker on my hand. Monday to Thursday I was a monk. Studied, slept early, felt amazing. Tonight after dinner I reinstalled one app, just to check a message from the class group. Then I thought, well, I've broken it anyway. So I reinstalled the game too. It's 1 am. I've played for four hours. Everything's back, and my History homework isn't done. I feel like a fraud. Kalyani Didi is going to ask tomorrow, and I don't know what to tell her. Maybe I'm just someone who can't do this.
Arnab

qa.q: What did Arnab write in marker on Monday?
How does Arnab feel at 1 am?
qa.a: Arnab feels like a fraud, ashamed and hopeless after one slip turned into four hours of gaming.

qa.q: What could Arnab try instead of a total ban?
qa.a: A smaller, realistic limit, such as one app for a set time each day, and treating a slip as one bad evening rather than a reason to give up.

qa.q: How might Kalyani Didi see the relapse?
qa.a: She may be disappointed but understanding, seeing that the all-or-nothing rule set Arnab up to fall.

grounding: A student's diary shows an all-or-nothing screen ban lasting four days before one slip is treated as total failure.
